svg.aria-label: How to write е, т: 2 letters, е, т, one after another
svg.title: Writing е, т
svg.desc: 2 letters written one after another: е, т (cyrillic). Each letter has its own group of frames; frame N of a group shows movements 1 to N of that letter, the movement being added drawn in ink over the finished letter, whose outline is read from _fonts/NotoSansCyrillic-Static.ttf. Each letter is drawn at its own scale from its own cited stroke order, so the strip does not show how large the letters are next to each other, how far apart they sit, or any join between them. Stroke order: е: RussianIrina, ‘Learning Russian - Alphabet letters, handwriting’, lowercase е demonstration, 02:26–02:30, YouTube, 5 February 2013 <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tqDLDfYoO2o>; т: RussianIrina, ‘Learning Russian - Alphabet letters, handwriting’, lowercase т demonstration, 07:29–07:36, YouTube, 5 February 2013 <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tqDLDfYoO2o>. Source notes on variation: е: The native-teacher video presents all 33 Russian letters first in print and then in the classic handwritten form taught at school. In the 02:26–02:30 lowercase е demonstration, the pen begins at the upper right, curves left around the upper loop, crosses through the middle, and continues counterclockwise around the rounded lower bowl in one continuous pen-down run, for zero intervening lifts. The demonstrated school hand is a tall open epsilon-like form with a small crossing loop at the middle; the bundled Noto Sans Cyrillic glyph is a compact printed e whose long middle bar reaches the open right side. This learner path preserves the source's upper-loop-to-middle-to-lower-bowl order and zero-lift evidence while fitting the printed form: curve around the upper bowl, sweep right along the middle bar, reverse through the junction, and circle the lower bowl without lifting. Connected cursive may add entry and exit joins, and individual handwriting may narrow, round, or slant either bowl differently. т: The native-teacher video presents all 33 Russian letters first in print and then in the classic handwritten form taught at school. In the 07:29–07:36 lowercase т demonstration, the pen begins at the upper left, descends the left stem, turns upward without lifting into a rounded first arch, descends the middle stem, rises through a rounded second arch, descends the right stem, and finishes through a small rising exit in one continuous pen-down run, for zero intervening lifts. The demonstrated school hand resembles a rounded Latin m with two arches and a rising exit; the bundled Noto Sans Cyrillic glyph is a printed T-shaped form with one central vertical stem and a horizontal top bar. This learner path preserves the source's initial-descent-before-joined-top-movements order and zero-lift evidence while fitting the printed outline: descend the central stem, retrace to the top junction, sweep left along the top bar, then retrace through the junction and sweep to the right tip without lifting. Connected cursive restores the source's two rounded arches and rising exit, and individual handwriting may round, narrow, widen, or slant the arches and stems differently.
svg.text: How it is written — 2 letters, one after another
Letter 1 of 2 — one unbroken stroke · 2 movements
Letter 2 of 2 — one unbroken stroke · 3 movements
Letter 1: stroke order after RussianIrina, ‘Learning Russian - Alphabet letters, handwriting’, lowercase е demonstration, 02:26–02:30, YouTube, 5 February
Letter 2: stroke order after RussianIrina, ‘Learning Russian - Alphabet letters, handwriting’, lowercase т demonstration, 07:29–07:36, YouTube, 5 February
This order is attested, not standardised; the source records where it varies.
